Brand Safety vs Brand Suitability: What They Cost You

By lowob · 15 July 2026 · 4-minute read · Distribution

Brand safety keeps ads away from harmful content; brand suitability keeps them near content that fits the brand. Both are enforced by blunt tools that over-block by default. Set standards from actual risk, prefer category controls to keyword lists, allow reputable news and review what was blocked.

Brand safety is the practice of keeping a company's ads away from content that would harm it by association: violence, hate, illegal activity, adult material, misinformation. Brand suitability is the narrower practice of keeping ads near content that fits the brand and away from content that is legal and harmless but wrong for it: a children's product beside crime reporting, a wealth product beside a story about layoffs.

Both matter. Both are also enforced by blunt tools that cost advertisers more reach than they realize.

How enforcement works

Keyword blocklists. Lists of words that, if present on a page, prevent the ad from serving. Simple, widespread, and crude: a blocklist containing "shooting" blocks a photography site, one containing "crash" blocks a report on a market recovery.

Category classification. Verification vendors classify pages into content categories and risk levels, and buyers choose which to allow. More precise than keywords, and dependent on the vendor's classifier.

Inclusion lists. The buyer specifies the sites and apps where ads may appear, rather than where they may not. The most protective approach and the one that most limits reach.

Pre-bid and post-bid verification. Pre-bid filters block an impression before the buyer bids; post-bid measures what happened after the ad served and, at best, refunds it. Pre-bid protects; post-bid reports.

What over-blocking costs

Blunt safety settings have defunded quality journalism, particularly news, by blocking ads on any page that mentions difficult subjects, which is most of the news. Studies by industry bodies have found that a large share of blocked news inventory was safe by any reasonable standard. The advertiser loses reach among engaged, affluent readers; the publisher loses revenue; and the budget flows instead toward content designed to trip no filter, which is often the made-for-advertising inventory that adds nothing.

The cost is invisible on the report, because the report shows what was blocked, not what was lost.

Setting standards that work

Start from what would actually harm the brand, not from a vendor's default list. Prefer category and risk-level controls over raw keyword lists, and review any keyword list for words that are only dangerous in a context. Use inclusion lists for the core buy and controlled category rules for the reach buy. Allow reputable news with sensible exclusions rather than excluding news wholesale. Review the blocked-inventory report monthly for false positives. And treat verification as a setting to be managed, not a box to be ticked.

The other direction: suitability for restricted categories

For companies in reviewed categories the question runs the other way as well. Publishers and platforms apply their own suitability rules to advertisers, and a financial or crypto product can be excluded from inventory by the publisher's standards regardless of the buyer's. That is another reason the band map matters: some of the inventory that appears open on a DSP is closed by the publisher when the ad arrives, and the rejection appears as low delivery rather than as a message.

The honest summary

Brand safety protects against a real, if rare, harm. Brand suitability is a judgment about fit that should be made by the brand, not by a default. Both are enforced by tools that block far more than they should when left alone. The buyer who manages them gains reach that competitors have blocked themselves out of, and the buyer who ignores them is paying for both the harm and the waste.

Brand safety avoids harm; brand suitability judges fit. Both are enforced by blunt tools that over-block by default. Set standards from actual risk, prefer categories to keywords, allow reputable news, and review what was blocked.

lowob takeaways

  • Keyword blocklists are crude: a list containing 'crash' can block a report on a market recovery.
  • Over-blocking has defunded quality news, and industry studies found much blocked news inventory was safe.
  • Publishers can exclude financial or crypto ads by their own rules, which shows up as low delivery rather than a message.
